summary: Describes opportunistic encryption, as designed and implemented by the Linux FreeS/WAN project, using IKE and IPsec. It lets systems encrypt traffic without prior arrangement, using DNS to distribute public keys, which resists passive attacks. DNSSEC protects against active ones. It reduces administration from growing with the square of the number of systems to linear. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Strangers can lock their messages without first meeting. They look up each other's public lock in the internet's phone book.

questions: how does opportunistic encryption use dns
how are gateways authorized in opportunistic encryption
subtitle: Encryption without prior arrangement, using DNS to distribute keys.

tldr.problem: Systems want to encrypt traffic without pre-arranging keys with their peers. Traditional approaches require either manual configuration or a trust infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: Opportunistic encryption uses IKE and IPsec to negotiate secure tunnels on demand, with public keys distributed through DNS. A receiving gateway looks up whether a destination supports encryption before forwarding traffic.
tldr.outcome: Two systems can communicate securely without prior arrangement. Administrative overhead drops from the square of the number of systems to linear growth. DNSSEC protects against active attacks.

today: RFC 4322 is Informational and describes the Linux FreeS/WAN implementation as of version 2.00. Later versions use RFC 3445 for improved key record handling. While the general concept of opportunistic encryption has merit, widespread deployment remains limited due to DNS reverse-map control issues and the complexity of managing opportunistic tunnels at scale.

sections.title: Opportunistic Encryption Concept
sections.content:
RFC 4322 describes a system where systems can encrypt traffic with arbitrary peers without any prior arrangement. Each system publishes its public key in DNS and enables opportunistic encryption in its IPsec stack. When one system sends traffic to another, the first system checks DNS to see if the destination supports encryption. If so, it negotiates keys using the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol and tunnels the traffic through IPsec. If not, traffic may proceed in the clear, depending on local policy.

This approach creates a fax effect: as more systems support opportunistic encryption, the value increases because more peers can be encrypted with. The Linux FreeS/WAN project developed this design as a practical way to make encryption the default, even between strangers.
sections.eli5: When Alice wants to send a message to Bob, she checks if Bob posted his public key online. If he did, they automatically start talking in a locked code. As more people post their keys, more conversations get locked automatically.

sections.title: How the System Works
sections.content:
The opportunistic encryption gateway decides for each datagram whether to encrypt and tunnel it by looking up the destination address in DNS. The gateway maintains a cache of source/destination pairs it has seen, along with the outcome of each encryption attempt: success, failure, or a negative result (encryption not available).

When a new flow arrives, the gateway performs a reverse DNS lookup (using the destination address in the in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa zones) to find a TXT delegation record. This record tells the gateway which security gateway to tunnel to and may provide the destination's public key. If encryption succeeds, the gateway creates an IPsec security association (SA). If it fails, the gateway either permits traffic in the clear (permissive mode) or drops it (paranoid mode), depending on policy. A timeout refreshes these cache entries periodically, allowing the gateway to discover changes in authorization policy.
sections.eli5: When Alice's mail carrier (gateway) sees a letter going to Bob, it checks: does Bob have a key posted? If yes, the carrier locks the letter and sends it to Bob's mail carrier. If no, the carriers decide whether to send it unlocked or throw it away.

sections.title: Peer Authentication and DNS
sections.content:
Without peer authentication, an attacker could intercept the key exchange and inject a forged public key. To prevent this, opportunistic encryption relies on DNSSEC. When DNSSEC is available, the receiver can verify that the public key it retrieved is authentic. When DNSSEC is not available, the receiver may only trust keys that delegate to their own address as a gateway (limiting potential redirects).

The system uses two DNS record types: KEY records hold the public RSA key of a security gateway in the reverse-map zone (e.g., 4.1.1.192.in-addr.arpa for gateway 192.1.1.4). TXT delegation records authorize a security gateway to act on behalf of an end system. For example, Alice publishes a TXT record at her address saying: X-IPsec-Server(10)=192.1.1.5 AQMM...3s1Q==, which means gateway 192.1.1.5 can speak for her with priority 10. The sender retrieves these records to authenticate the peer and verify authorization.
sections.eli5: Before locking the letter, the mail carrier checks: is the recipient's key really theirs? DNSSEC is like a notary stamp that proves the key is genuine. Without it, the carrier only trusts keys that match the recipient's own address, not ones that point elsewhere.

sections.title: Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
Opportunistic encryption faces practical obstacles. Not all administrators control their reverse DNS. A system without reverse DNS control can use a Fully-Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) in phase 1 negotiation instead, but this requires the forward-map DNS to have the gateway's public KEY record. Mobile systems (those with dynamic IP addresses) can use FQDN IDs to avoid reverse-map dependencies.

Network Address Translation (NAT) adds complexity: a gateway co-located with NAT must translate addresses before encryption to use the translated address in phase 2. If the gateway is behind NAT, IPsec tunnel mode still works, but normal NAT traversal issues apply. Systems using the same gateway (multi-homing) can use multiple TXT delegation records with equal priority, allowing load sharing, though choosing among multiple tunnels at the receiving end remains application-specific.

Key rollover requires care: new keys must propagate through DNS caches (controlled by the MINIMUM field in SOA records, often hours or days) before being used for new encryption. The system generates a new key pair well in advance and publishes both old and new keys in DNS, allowing receivers to verify signatures from either one until the old key ages out.
sections.eli5: Not everyone controls their mailbox's address book. Some systems have to use a domain name instead. Shared mail carriers have to pick which of several of them to use. And when a carrier gets a new lock, it has to wait for address books to update before using it.

sections.title: Security Tradeoffs
sections.content:
Opportunistic tunnels lack the trust properties of configured (pre-arranged) tunnels. Configured tunnels may bypass firewalls or receive priority treatment. Opportunistic tunnels must not receive any special privileges and MUST NOT bypass ordinary firewalling rules. The receiving gateway MUST use ingress filtering to ensure that datagrams from the tunnel match the agreed-upon source and destination addresses from the negotiation. This prevents one peer from impersonating another.

DNSSEC is critical: without it, opportunistic encryption resists passive eavesdropping but not active man-in-the-middle attacks where an attacker substitutes a forged public key. Denial of service is also a risk: an attacker can attempt to create phase 1 security associations with any system, consuming resources. The IKE design mitigates some DoS attacks through cookies, but the system must be prepared to negotiate with arbitrary peers.

DNS failures present a choice: permissive mode allows traffic to go in the clear if DNS fails or returns no record, while paranoid mode drops the traffic. This is a local policy decision because some networks lack properly configured reverse-maps and cannot afford complete isolation.
sections.eli5: Locked mail from strangers gets no special treatment. Firewalls still check it. Without a notary stamp (DNSSEC), a clever attacker can fake a key. And too many people trying to set up locks at once can bog down the system.
